#4381. 10 Details That Show Rockstar Went Above and Beyond With GTA VI

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

Rockstar has made some amazing games over the years, and one thing that always remains the same is that the team has an amazing attention to detail. The maps are massive, full of life, have tons of activities, and even have insane levels of detail that you would never even think to look at.

A small instance of this can be seen in Arthur Morgan, as his hair grows, can be cut, and even styled. It is easy to see why Rockstar often gets praise from gamers. However, now it is time for GTA VI to shine.

Like before, Rockstar has definitely gone above and beyond with the attention to detail, and this is just part of the reason why GTA VI is a great game.

Ah yes, just when I am trying to get any work done, I turn to my phone, pick it up, and start flipping through social media. Specifically, I start swiping through shorts on YouTube or reels on Instagram.

If you are addicted to doomscrolling through life like many people in the world, the good news is that you can do that in GTA VI. Rockstar has never shied away from emulating life in some aspects of each of their games, and this time, you can use the Snapmatic app in GTA VI to scroll through posts and viral clips.

Of course, this has a connection to the actual gameplay, and no, you can’t become a viral star in GTA VI, but it does show the level of detail Rockstar is going for in the game, as the feed gets updated. Just don’t doomscroll very long.

The wanted system has evolved over the years that the Grand Theft Auto series has existed, but it has never been this detailed. Previously, if you became wanted, you could simply hide, wait out the cops, and leave when they forget you exist.

Now, the cops remember you. They know what you look like, whether you were with a partner, what car you drive, and the clothes you wear. Each of these gets marked, and you need to take care of them if you want to avoid detection.

If they know your outfit, you need to change. If they know your car, you need to get a new one. If you don’t wear a mask, they will know your face. It is a level of detail never seen in the wanted system.

Grand Theft Auto V had a decent number of buildings you could enter, with the total being roughly around 100. Still, when you are living in a city, that number is pretty small and mostly impressive by game standards.

Grand Theft Auto VI takes this to a new level, and it shows how dedicated Rockstar is to going above and beyond with detail, as it is estimated that 70% of the buildings are enterable. The confirmed number by the mapping community based on trailers and available data is sitting at around 400, that is already over four times the number in the previous game.

It is amazing that Rockstar has taken the time and energy to put in so many details and fully flesh out all of these buildings.

GTA Online 2.0 will be coming eventually, and there are some changes that Rockstar should make.

Leonida is based on Florida, and if you have ever been to Florida, you know that there is a lot of wildlife there. Venture outside of the city, and you can find numerous animals living in the wetlands.

Rockstar made sure to go above and beyond when it comes to the game’s animals with the team putting in more than 170 different animal species. This includes over 60 bird species, 30 land mammals, and also various aquatic life and reptiles.

For context, Grand Theft Auto V has around 28 different animal species, and Red Dead Redemption 2 has over 200. Leonida will be just as wild as the real Florida.

The Grand Theft Auto series obviously has a large emphasis on committing crimes, with each game giving you the ability to rob stores, steal cars, and more. However, none of the previous titles have the same level of detail when it comes to committing a crime.

GTA VI has multiple options when committing a crime. Will you wear a mask? Do you want to bring a partner? Are you going to use a silencer on your weapon? This all plays into whether you get caught in the act and how the police respond.

On top of this, other crimes like stealing a car are now more detailed as well, with you having the ability to bust windows or even use tools to pop locks. Some cars even have trackers. You can even use an app to determine a car’s resale value.

It is easy to overlook NPCs in a video game unless you are directly interacting with them. All the people on the street tend to blur together at times, but when you stop to take a look, you will see various NPCs that look alike.

In GTA V, it is estimated that there are around 800 unique NPCs roaming the streets of Los Santos and beyond. However, when tested, players have shown it doesn’t take very long to run into the same NPC but in a different location.

Let’s scale this up to GTA VI. There isn’t an official number yet, but Rockstar has stated that the NPCs will be far more diverse, with they varying in height and weight. They will also have defining details like birthmarks, moles, skin conditions, and more. Even the sizes of their muscles, butts, and chests can differ. That’s a lot of detail.

The weather often gets crazy down in Florida. It is normal for residents of the state to deal with torrential downpours, strong winds, tropical storms, and even hurricanes. In other words, you can’t expect Leonida to not have similar weather.

GameInformer detailed some of the weather effects that will be in GTA VI, and according to them, there will be tropical storms and hurricanes that make “water gush off roof edges and lamposts,” and make it so “everything is dripping wet.”

This means that you will need to unleash your inner Florida Man and run through a hurricane to see what happens. Maybe you will get tossed around. I just hope Rockstar captured the downpour that seems to happen every day around 3pm.

GTA 6 features a completely rebuilt dynamic wind and atmospheric system designed to bring the tropical world of Leonida to life like never before.

Being a Rockstar game, there is a degree of change that can be expected to happen to your character. This didn’t exist in GTA V, but in Red Dead Redemption 2, Arthur Morgan’s weight could change, his hair could grow and be cut, and his face changes.

Rockstar has taken this a step further for GTA VI, as you have two protagonists, and both of them can have their appearance change over time. Overeating causes weight gain, undereating causes weight loss, working out makes your muscles grow, and much more.

The protagonists aren’t just static characters that don’t change with time, they evolve and grow. Their hair also grows and needs to be cut. This level of detail is above and beyond what happens in a normal game.

While GTA V is great, the NPCs in that game are pretty lackluster. When you commit a crime, they mostly switch between two actions; fight or run. Mostly, they run away from guns, car crashes, or whatever else.

The NPCs in GTA VI, however, act much differently. They are more lifelike. They will take out their phones to record you. You can listen in on conversations, and the NPCs will get angry if they spot you. The NPCs will go so far as to remember you.

This means that if you continuously wreak havoc in Leonida, the NPCs will act differently towards you. Some may even be hostile as soon as they see you. A lot of work goes into making NPCs feel lifelike, and Rockstar is going above and beyond with it.

If it wasn’t obvious already, GTA VI is about a couple named Lucia and Jason. The pair are trying to create a better life and get out of crime. A big part of the game revolves around their relationship.

The couple can spend time together, furthering their bond. They can play games like mini-golf, go scuba diving together, and much more. The more they spend time together, the stronger their bond will become.

Rockstar put a lot of detail in just the relationship aspect of the game, with your partner messaging you throughout the day to check in and more. You actually need to care about who you commit crime with, as if you don’t your relationship will fail and affect the story.

The Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks have revealed some interesting details about the game, such as new mechanics and changes to the menus.

#4380. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

#4378. Magic mushrooms rewire the brain in a way scientists didn't expect

A new study from the University of California, Santa Cruz, has revealed how psilocybin, the psychedelic substance found in "magic mushrooms," changes the brain by reorganizing connections between nerve cells. The findings could eventually help scientists develop treatments for mental health conditions that capture some of psilocybin's potential benefits without producing hallucinations.

The research, published October 15 in Nature Neuroscience, found that psilocybin rapidly encourages brain cells to form new connections and helps those connections mature. At the same time, it promotes the removal of certain older connections, suggesting that its effects involve more than simply increasing communication between neurons.

Experiments in mice also revealed something especially intriguing. The researchers were able to separate the cellular changes responsible for this rewiring from a behavioral response commonly associated with psychedelic effects. This suggests that some of psilocybin's effects on brain structure may be achievable without the hallucinations typically associated with the drug.

The discovery could provide a foundation for developing medications that enhance the brain's ability to adapt and reorganize itself, a property known as neuroplasticity. Such treatments might eventually offer new approaches for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and other psychiatric conditions.

The team also identified a particular group of neurons in the cerebral cortex that plays an essential role in psilocybin's effects on brain connections. Importantly, the researchers discovered that the drug does not affect every brain in the same way. Its influence depends partly on whether the brain has previously experienced chronic stress.

"I consider this work a major advance, particularly in our understanding of how psilocybin reshapes neural circuits and its potential implications for treating mental disorders," said senior author Yi Zuo, professor of molecular, cell, and developmental biology at UC Santa Cruz.

Why Scientists Are Taking a New Look at Psychedelics

Scientific interest in psychedelic drugs has changed dramatically over the past century. During the middle of the 20th century, substances such as psilocybin and LSD attracted attention from Western researchers because of their powerful effects on perception, consciousness, and mood.

Early studies suggested these compounds might have applications in psychiatric treatment. However, scientific investigations slowed substantially after the United States passed the Controlled Substances Act in 1970, which imposed strict restrictions on these substances.

In recent years, researchers have renewed their interest in psychedelics, particularly their ability to produce rapid and potentially lasting changes in brain function.

Scientists sometimes describe these compounds as "psychoplastogens" because they can stimulate neuroplasticity after a single dose. Neuroplasticity refers to the brain's capacity to change its structure and activity by forming, strengthening, reorganizing, or removing connections between neurons.

This property is particularly interesting for mental health treatment because conditions such as depression can involve disruptions in the circuits responsible for regulating mood, emotions, and behavior.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has previously recognized the therapeutic potential of psychedelic research by granting Breakthrough Therapy designations to substances including psilocybin and MDMA. These designations are intended to accelerate the development and review of promising treatments for serious medical conditions.

In September 2026, the FDA took another step toward evaluating psychedelic treatments by organizing a public hearing titled "Considerations for Potential Future Therapeutic Use of Psychedelic Drugs."

Experts discussed how healthcare professionals administering psychedelic treatments should be qualified, how potential risks could be managed through Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) programs, and how future clinical trials should be designed.

As regulators examine ways psychedelic treatments might eventually become part of mainstream healthcare, researchers are increasingly focused on understanding exactly what these substances do to the brain. Identifying the cellular mechanisms behind their effects could help scientists develop treatments that are both effective and safer to administer.

To investigate how psilocybin changes brain structure, the UC Santa Cruz team used an advanced imaging method called two-photon microscopy.

This technology allows scientists to observe extremely small structures inside living tissue with remarkable detail. Using it, the researchers followed individual connections on neurons in living mice over several weeks, allowing them to see how those structures changed after psilocybin treatment.

Their attention centered on tiny projections called dendritic spines. These structures extend from neurons and receive messages from neighboring nerve cells. They help form synapses, the specialized junctions through which neurons communicate.

Synapses are essential for processing information and supporting functions such as learning, memory, and emotional regulation. Changes in their number, strength, and organization can alter the way information travels through the brain.

Within just 24 hours of psilocybin administration, the researchers observed a substantial increase in newly forming dendritic spines.

But the drug did more than encourage new connections to appear. It also helped them develop into more mature structures at an unusually rapid pace.

Normally, newly formed spines often begin as small, immature structures described as "stubby." Many remain unstable and disappear before becoming fully developed connections.

After psilocybin treatment, however, a much larger proportion developed into structures with a distinctive "mushroom" appearance. These mature spines are generally more stable and contain higher concentrations of receptors that receive chemical signals from neighboring neurons.

Because of these features, mature spines can support stronger and more persistent communication between brain cells, potentially contributing to lasting changes in circuits involved in memory and mood.

For lead author Jacob Baker, one of the biggest questions is whether these structural changes require the intense psychedelic experience typically produced by psilocybin.

"Psychedelics are fascinating compounds because they have the potential to profoundly transform who we are by reshaping the neural circuits in our brains," said Baker, a Ph.D. student in Zuo's lab.

"These newly formed connections can integrate into existing neural circuitry and persist over time, leaving a lasting structural trace of psilocybin's effects on the brain."

Psilocybin Affects Healthy and Stressed Brains Differently

One of the study's most revealing findings was that psilocybin's influence on brain connections changed depending on whether the mice had experienced prolonged stress.

In healthy mice, psilocybin initially stimulated the formation of new dendritic spines. Over the following three weeks, however, the number of connections gradually moved back toward its previous level.

This happened partly because the brain eliminated some connections that had existed before treatment. Rather than simply accumulating additional synapses, the healthy brain appeared to reorganize its existing circuitry while maintaining an overall balance.

The researchers observed a different response in mice exposed to chronic stress.

To investigate this, they used an unpredictable mild stress model, which exposes animals to varying low-intensity stressors and produces changes that resemble certain features of human depression.

Prolonged stress is known to interfere with neural communication and can cause substantial losses of synaptic connections. Over time, these changes can weaken the circuits involved in important brain functions.

When the stressed mice received psilocybin, the researchers observed an especially strong increase in the formation of new dendritic spines.

At the same time, psilocybin prevented the unusually high rate of connection loss associated with chronic stress.

Together, these effects suggest that psilocybin may do more than temporarily increase the number of connections in the brain. Under stressful conditions, it may also help preserve existing connections and restore circuitry that has been disrupted.

"These findings challenge the prevailing view that psilocybin simply increases neural connectivity and suggest that its effects depend on the brain's underlying condition," Zuo added.

"This provides a new perspective on how psychedelics might help restore neural circuits disrupted by stress, with potentially important implications for understanding their therapeutic effects in depression and other psychiatric disorders."

Could Psilocybin Rewire the Brain Without Hallucinations?

Perhaps the most significant implication of the research concerns a longstanding question in psychedelic medicine: Are hallucinations and altered states of consciousness necessary for the brain changes that might contribute to therapeutic benefits?

To explore this possibility, the scientists examined the role of serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2ARs), which are proteins on the surfaces of cells that respond to chemical signals. These receptors are central to the effects of psilocybin and other classic psychedelics.

The researchers focused on a group of nerve cells called Layer 5 pyramidal neurons. These cells are located in the cerebral cortex, the outer region of the brain involved in complex functions such as perception, reasoning, and decision-making.

Layer 5 pyramidal neurons serve as important communication pathways that send information from the cortex to other brain regions. They also contain high levels of serotonin 2A receptors, making them especially relevant to understanding psilocybin's effects.

Using genetically modified mice, the team selectively changed whether these neurons possessed the receptors.

The results revealed a striking separation between changes in brain connections and a behavior associated with psychedelic activity.

When the researchers restored serotonin 2A receptors only in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin was still able to stimulate the development of new synapses and help stabilize them.

Surprisingly, these mice did not display the characteristic head twitch response that researchers commonly use as an indicator of psychedelic activity in rodents.

The scientists then performed the opposite experiment.

When they removed serotonin 2A receptors specifically from Layer 5 pyramidal neurons, psilocybin lost its ability to stimulate the same structural growth of synapses.

However, the mice still exhibited the head twitch response.

These contrasting results demonstrate that serotonin 2A receptor signaling in Layer 5 pyramidal neurons is necessary and sufficient for the structural brain changes observed in the experiments, while those same receptors are not required for the psychedelic-associated behavioral response.

In other words, the cellular pathway responsible for psilocybin's brain rewiring can be separated from the pathway responsible for this particular behavioral marker of psychedelic activity.

Because mice cannot describe subjective experiences, the head twitch response does not directly establish whether an animal is experiencing hallucinations. Nevertheless, the findings provide important evidence that these two effects involve distinct cellular mechanisms.

A Potential Path Toward Psychedelic Treatments Without the Trip

The discovery could have major implications for the development of future psychiatric medications.

If researchers can identify compounds that activate the brain's ability to rebuild and reorganize neural connections without triggering psychedelic effects, it may become possible to create treatments that preserve some of psilocybin's therapeutic potential while avoiding the need for patients to undergo intense altered states of consciousness.

Such medications could be easier to administer and might require less intensive clinical supervision than conventional psychedelic-assisted therapies.

"By showing that therapeutic circuit remodeling and hallucinogenic effects operate through distinct cellular pathways, our study provides a promising blueprint for designing non-hallucinogenic drug analogs," Zuo said.

"Such therapeutics could deliver the fast and lasting antidepressant benefits of psychedelics while eliminating hallucinogenic side effects -- making neuroplasticity treatments safer, more scalable, and accessible to a broader patient population."

Although the results are promising, the experiments were conducted in mice. Additional research will be necessary to determine whether the same cellular mechanisms operate in humans and whether separating brain rewiring from psychedelic effects can produce effective treatments for depression, PTSD, or other psychiatric disorders.

For now, the findings provide a more detailed picture of how psilocybin changes the brain and reveal a potential strategy for harnessing its effects on neural connections without relying on the psychedelic experience itself.

The study's other UC Santa Cruz coauthors include molecular and cell biologists Jacob Baker, Emily Kogan, Shaorong Ma, and Ju Lu, alongside Zuo.

Funding came from the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute on Aging. The psilocybin used in the experiments was supplied through the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) Drug Supply Program.

#4377. 2027 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter

See all results for new 2027 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter for sale near 37040

Seeing the Mercedes-Benz badge affixed to the front of a large commercial van feels, well, wrong, but the Sprinter van is a global leader in cargo hauling. It’s anything but a luxury-oriented Mercedes, instead focusing on package delivery and worksite practicality. A 170-hp diesel inline-four is standard, as is rear-wheel drive. A more powerful 211-hp version of the diesel is available and can be had with all-wheel drive.

The Sprinter is offered in several configurations: the Cargo Van model has seating for two and a crazy amount of cargo capacity behind the front seats. The Passenger Van variant can be had with up to five rows of seats to maximize people space. The Crew Van splits the difference and comes with two rows of seats with plenty of room behind the second row for your team’s tools of the trade.

Expert Tip: If you’re interested in an electric cargo van, Mercedes-Benz also makes the eSprinter, but we review that model separately.

Compare the 2027 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

The entry-level Worker trim for the Sprinter Cargo Van has been discontinued. Otherwise, the Sprinter carries over to 2027 without any other significant changes.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

Every Sprinter, save for the electric eSprinter, relies on diesel fuel. The base engine is a turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder rated for 170 horsepower and 295 pound-feet of torque. The optional high-output engine is good for 211 ponies and 332 pound-feet. Both feed a nine-speed automatic transmission. All-wheel drive is available only with the higher-output engine.

While not as potent as the 310-hp EcoBoost V-6 in the Ford Transit or the 401-hp V-8 in the GMC Savana, the Sprinter's diesels offer adequate thrust. Though no van boasts razor-sharp handling, the Sprinter's standard load-adaptive stability control and available crosswind-assist systems help keep it out of trouble in dicey situations.

In Comparison: Though we've yet to strap our test equipment to a recent Sprinter, we can tell you this is not a quick vehicle. We'd guess the base model would need 13.5 seconds to reach 60 mph, while the higher-output model might take 12.0. For reference, the Ford Transit can complete the same sprint in as little as 6.7 seconds.

The Sprinter can tow up to 7500 pounds when equipped with the high-output engine. Models with the 170-hp four-cylinder are good for 5000 pounds, though wheelbase and other specs can affect that cap.

The Sprinter's maximum payload is 6812 pounds. In order to reach that figure, you'll have to spec the cargo van with the heavy-duty 4500 chassis, the standard roof, the 144-inch wheelbase, rear-wheel drive, and the high-output engine. Crew models can carry as much as 3825 pounds, while the passenger van's hauling capacity tops out at 3307 pounds.

The EPA doesn't require automakers to submit fuel-economy data for full-size vans, nor does it publish such information. When we take a Sprinter on our 200-mile real-world highway fuel economy route, we'll update this section with the results.

First Row: Like other full-size vans, the entry-level Sprinter is spartan inside, but the driver's seat is heated, cruise control comes standard, and Benz offers several extra-cost upgrades to improve comfort, convenience, and driver safety.

Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Rows: The Sprinter cargo van has no seats after the driver and front passenger, but the Crew model gets a three-seat second row. Standard-length (144-inch) passenger vans can comfortably accommodate 12 people across four rows, while the 170-incher passenger van seats 15 across five rows.

Cargo Capacity: The cargo van offers up to 533 cubic feet of space for whatever you need to haul. Crew vans can swallow a max of 396 cubes, while the passenger van (when fully occupied) tops out at 117 cubic feet.

The Sprinter is not your typical Mercedes. It's built for utility first and foremost, which helps explain the base model's underwhelming tech setup. Mercedes provides an AM/FM radio that plays through five speakers (13 in passenger vans).

Shoppers can option a 10.3-inch touchscreen, though, and that system supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connections.

The majority of the Sprinter's driver-assistance features are optional, not standard.

For information about the Sprinter's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Sprinter's limited warranty is typical for the class, but its powertrain coverage is longer than most. Mercedes doesn't include scheduled maintenance.

#4376. Battlefield 6 may have actually done it: beaten Call of Duty

Battlefield 6 sales are setting all kinds of records, but one in particular has long eluded the Battlefield series.

If you’ve been paying any attention to the shooter market these past few months, you won’t be surprised to learn that Battlefield 6 has been an unprecedented success for EA, and the Battlefield series as a whole.

The game managed to sell over 7 million units at launch, climbing to the top of the charts anywhere you look, including setting new series concurrent player records on Steam. Thanks to new data, we now better understand the true scale of this launch.

The latest Circana report, which looks at game and hardware sales in the United States, has arrived. This iteration covers the month of October, which is when Battlefield 6 was released.

Battlefield 6 was the top-selling game across all platforms during October - which isn’t surprising. It has overtaken NBA 2K26 to become 2025’s best-selling game year-to-date, making it the best-selling Battlefield game ever.

In October alone, the game sold more than the lifetime sales of Battlefield 1, previously the best-selling entry in the franchise.

Battlefield 6 even set records beyond just its own series, having now produced the highest single-month dollar sales (physical and digital) total for any full game released in the last three years. The previous record holder was 2022’s Modern Warfare 2.

November’s report, which is set to arrive midway through December, will show, once and for all, whether Battlefield 6 has been able to overtake Black Ops 7. With one exception, Call of Duty games have, for more than a decade, topped the best-selling year-to-date chart. Regardless of the quality of the individual titles, or the competition in any given year, nothing has been able to shake that dominance.

Given all this momentum, Battlefield 6 has a shot at dethroning Call of Duty this year, beating Black Ops 7 to become the year’s best-seller. You never want to count out the sheer popularity of Call of Duty among casual players, however, which is what’s going to make December’s report all the more interesting.
